nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; the Victorian detective story and historical romance
literary_identity: Physician and writer; the creator of Sherlock Holmes and the founder of the modern detective story.
biography: Born in Edinburgh on 22 May 1859 into an Irish Catholic family of artists; educated at Stonyhurst and the University of Edinburgh, where he qualified in medicine in 1881. He practised as a ship's surgeon and then in Southsea, and published A Study in Scarlet in Beeton's Christmas Annual in 1887; the Holmes stories were commissioned by the Strand Magazine from 1891, and the character became a national institution, which Doyle attempted to kill off in 1893 and was forced to revive in 1903. The historical novels Micah Clarke (1889), The White Company (1891), Rodney Stone (1896) and Sir Nigel (1906), the Brigadier Gerard stories and The Lost World (1912) show the range he claimed for himself. He served as a volunteer physician in the Boer War, wrote The Great Boer War (1900) and The War in South Africa (1902), and campaigned for spiritualism for the last twenty years of his life. He died at Crowborough, Sussex, on 7 July 1930.
literary_profile: Doyle invented the detective story as a modern genre: the Holmes stories are constructed as a problem and a solution, with a narrator who is intelligent but not deductive, and a detective whose method is observation combined with an encyclopedia of specialised knowledge. The stories are also a document of late-Victorian London — the hansom, the gaslight, the chemical laboratory, the colonial return, the country house and the bank — and their form (the short story sequence with a stable pair of characters) became the template of the modern series.
stylistic_characteristics: The clue and the deduction; the Watson narrator as the reader's stand-in; the opening problem and the explanatory retrospect; the adventure story's energy and the historical novel's scholarship; the plain, lucid narrative prose; the repertory of characters and the mythical London.
intellectual_concerns: Rationality and method against mystery; crime, class and the colonial fortune; the imperial frontier and the war; honour, courage and the gentleman; the supernatural (in his later work) against the scientific; the professional man and his expertise.
historical_significance: Doyle created the most famous character in English fiction and the form of the modern detective story: Holmes and Watson are the origin of the mystery series, and the Holmes canon is a central document of Victorian London. His historical novels were considered by their author his best work, and The Lost World founded the modern science-fiction adventure.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Victorian and Edwardian scientific romance
literary_identity: Novelist, scientific romancer and social prophet; the inventor of the modern scientific romance and one of the most influential English writers of the twentieth century.
biography: Born at Bromley on 21 September 1866, son of a shopkeeper and a professional cricketer's daughter; he was apprenticed to a draper, won a scholarship to the Normal School of Science in South Kensington in 1884, and was taught biology by T. H. Huxley, an experience that made him a lifelong evolutionist. He taught science and wrote for the Saturday Review before The Time Machine (1895) made him famous; The Island of Doctor Moreau (1896), The Invisible Man (1897), The War of the Worlds (1898), When the Sleeper Wakes (1899) and The First Men in the Moon (1901) followed, and from 1900 he turned to the social novels (Kipps, Tono-Bungay, The History of Mr Polly) and to the utopian and prophetic works (A Modern Utopia, The Outline of History, The Shape of Things to Come). He joined the Fabian Society in 1903 and quarrelled with the Webbs, and he died in London on 13 August 1946.
literary_profile: Wells took the evolutionary biology he had learned from Huxley and made it the basis of a new kind of fiction: the scientific romance, which uses an invention or a discovery as the premise for a realistic narrative of its social and psychological consequences. His early romances are single-conceit stories carried by a precise, journalistic specification of detail, and their subject is the fragility of the human species, the possibility of degeneration and the relative insignificance of man in time. After 1900 he wrote the 'novel of ideas' as social criticism, aiming to make fiction an instrument of reform.
stylistic_characteristics: The single scientific premise developed to its consequences; precise technical and topographical detail; a first-person witness narrator; the sudden perspective change (the Martian view of England, the Eloi of the far future); a plain, fast, journalistic narrative; the epigram and the Utopian debate in the later novels.
intellectual_concerns: Time, evolutionary deep time and the fate of the species; the machine and the alienation of labour; imperialism reversed (the Martians as colonisers); science, experiment and moral responsibility; class division and the Eloi/Morlock image; utopia, progress and the possibility of catastrophe.
historical_significance: Wells founded modern science fiction: The Time Machine, The War of the Worlds and The Island of Doctor Moreau are the foundational texts of the genre, and their images — the time traveller, the Martian cylinder, the Morlocks, the invisible man — became permanent English myths. His social novels and his Outline of History made him one of the most widely read writers in the world, and his influence on Huxley, Orwell, Stapledon and the whole twentieth-century literature of the future is direct.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; Transcendentalist essay, lecture and poetry
literary_identity: Essayist, lecturer and poet; the central figure of American Transcendentalism and the first American writer to make a philosophy of self-reliance a national literature.
biography: Born in Boston on 25 May 1803, the son of a Unitarian minister; he was educated at Harvard and at the Divinity School, was ordained in 1829, and resigned his Boston pastorate in 1832 over his refusal to administer the Lord's Supper. He travelled in Europe in 1833, met Carlyle, Coleridge and Wordsworth, and settled at Concord. Nature appeared anonymously in 1836; the Divinity School Address of 1838 made him notorious, and the Essays (1841, 1844) made him famous. He edited The Dial (1840-44), lectured across the northern states for forty years, and died at Concord on 27 April 1882.
literary_profile: Emerson invented the American essay: informal, oracular, built of separate paragraphs that circle a subject rather than argue it through, and addressed to the individual reader's own intuitions. His subject is the divinity of the self and of nature, the rejection of institutions and the authority of the present moment, and the call to original work. He was the intellectual centre of the Concord circle and the man who made American writing independent of Europe.
stylistic_characteristics: The aphoristic paragraph; abrupt transitions and serial assertion; the lecture as literary form; symbolic uses of nature; the first-person plural of address; images drawn from science, Plato and the Orient.
intellectual_concerns: Self-reliance and the divinity of the individual; nature as revelation; the rejection of institutional religion; the American scholar and the nation's intellectual independence; representative men and the uses of great persons; fate, compensation and the moral law.
historical_significance: Emerson is the founding philosopher of American literature: 'Nature', 'Self-Reliance', 'The American Scholar' and the Divinity School Address created the vocabulary of American individualism, and his influence runs through Thoreau, Whitman, Dickinson, Nietzsche, William James and the whole tradition of American pragmatism.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Nature (1836; published anonymously); The American Scholar (address, 1837); An Address Delivered before the Senior Class in Divinity College, Cambridge (1838); Essays: First Series (1841); Essays: Second Series (1844); Poems (1847); Representative Men (1850); English Traits (1856); The Conduct of Life (1860); May-Day and Other Pieces (1867); Society and Solitude (1870); Letters and Social Aims (1876); The Journals of Ralph Waldo Emerson, 10 vols (1909-14, posthumous); The Early Lectures, 3 vols (1959-72, posthumous).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the nature essay, the journal and the political essay
literary_identity: Essayist, naturalist and surveyor; the author of Walden and 'Civil Disobedience', the two founding texts of American nature writing and of the literature of conscience.
biography: Born at Concord, Massachusetts, on 12 July 1817; he was educated at Harvard and taught school, worked in his father's pencil factory, and from 1841 lived for periods in Emerson's household. He built his cabin at Walden Pond in 1845 and lived there two years, wrote 'Civil Disobedience' after spending a night in jail for refusing to pay a poll tax in 1846, and afterwards made several excursions to Maine, Cape Cod and Canada. He published A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers (1849) and Walden (1854), and died of tuberculosis at Concord on 6 May 1862.
literary_profile: Thoreau wrote the American sentence as a form of attention: his prose is exact, sinewy and full of puns, and his great subject is the disciplined perception of the natural world as a way of living rightly. Walden is at once a practical account of a two-year experiment in economy and a spiritual autobiography, and 'Civil Disobedience' is the founding modern argument that individual conscience outranks the state. His Journal, of over two million words, is the greatest American nature diary.
stylistic_characteristics: Concrete, comma-heavy cumulative sentences; exact measurement and enumeration; pun, paradox and irony; the excursion narrative; the journal entry developed as an art form; quotations from classical and Eastern texts.
intellectual_concerns: Nature and the discipline of attention; simplicity and economic independence; civil disobedience and the individual against the state; slavery and the fugitive; the seasons and the local landscape; reading, the classics and self-culture.
historical_significance: Thoreau is the founding figure of American nature writing and of the literature of non-violent resistance: Walden shaped the modern environmental movement, 'Civil Disobedience' influenced Tolstoy, Gandhi and Martin Luther King, and the Journal is one of the great unread works of the nineteenth century.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers (1849); 'Resistance to Civil Government' (1849; later 'Civil Disobedience'); Walden; or, Life in the Woods (1854); 'Slavery in Massachusetts' (1854); 'A Plea for Captain John Brown' (1859); Excursions (1863, posthumous); The Maine Woods (1864, posthumous); Cape Cod (1865, posthumous); A Yankee in Canada (1866, posthumous); Letters to Various Persons (1865, posthumous); The Journal (1906, 14 vols, posthumous).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Transcendentalist essay, criticism and the feminist treatise
literary_identity: Critic, editor and feminist; the first woman to work as a professional literary critic in the United States and the author of Woman in the Nineteenth Century.
biography: Born Sarah Margaret Fuller at Cambridgeport, Massachusetts, on 23 May 1810, and educated by her father in the classics. She taught at Bronson Alcott's school, edited The Dial (1840-42), translated Goethe, and wrote for Horace Greeley's New-York Tribune from 1844, becoming the paper's first woman correspondent. In Europe she met Mazzini and aroused the admiration of the young Emerson circle; she married the Italian revolutionary Giovanni Angelo Ossoli in 1847 and supported the Roman Republic in 1849. She drowned with her husband and son when the ship carrying them to America was wrecked off Fire Island on 19 July 1850.
literary_profile: Fuller wrote the most important American feminist argument before the Civil War: Woman in the Nineteenth Century turns the 'woman question' into a question of the self's right to develop, and it made her the first woman in America to command the authority of a public intellectual. Her criticism is the first substantial American body of writing on literature by a professional critic, and her dispatches from Italy are among the finest American war reportage of the century.
stylistic_characteristics: Conversational, digressive and allusive prose; the critical survey; the dialogue and the 'Conversation' as form; quotation and translation; the impassioned direct address of the feminist argument.
intellectual_concerns: The right of women to self-development and to intellectual life; democracy and the 'greatness' of the modern era; American literature and national culture; European revolutions and Italian freedom; the dignity of the woman artist; Transcendentalist religion.
historical_significance: Fuller is the founding figure of American feminism and the first professional woman of letters in the United States: Woman in the Nineteenth Century gave the American women's movement its first intellectual charter, and her Tribune criticism made literary journalism a serious American form. Her death off Fire Island made her a permanent figure of American legend.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Introduction to the Dial (1840-42); Summer on the Lakes, in 1843 (1844); Woman in the Nineteenth Century (1845); Papers on Literature and Art (1846); Memoirs of Margaret Fuller Ossoli (1852, posthumous); At Home and Abroad (1856, posthumous); Life Without and Life Within (1859, posthumous); These Sad but Glorious Days: Dispatches from Europe, 1846-1850 (1992, posthumous).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the romance, the tale and the literature of the Puritan past
literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the first great American novelist and the master of the American romance.
biography: Born in Salem, Massachusetts, on 4 July 1804, into a family descended from a judge of the 1692 witch trials; he was educated at Bowdoin College, where his friends were Longfellow and Franklin Pierce. He published Twice-Told Tales in 1837 after twelve years of solitary apprenticeship, worked in the Boston customs house and the Salem custom house, and published The Scarlet Letter in 1850, followed by The House of the Seven Gables (1851), The Blithedale Romance (1852) and The Marble Faun (1860). He was American consul at Liverpool in 1853-57 and died at Plymouth, New Hampshire, on 19 May 1864.
literary_profile: Hawthorne wrote the American romance as an enquiry into guilt: his subject is the inward consequence of sin, the secret life of the respectable, and the relation of the present to a Puritan past that will not let it go. His method is allegory handled with great psychological delicacy — the scarlet letter, the birthmark, the house of seven gables — and his prose is a cool, deliberate, faintly ironic instrument for the analysis of conscience.
stylistic_characteristics: Allegory with psychological depth; the single emblem around which a story is built; the romance of the 'neutral territory' between the real and the imaginary; the narrator's ironic commentary; the long retrospective sentence; the New England past as a haunting.
intellectual_concerns: Sin, guilt and the conscience; the Puritan inheritance and the witch trials; secrecy and the divided life; the artist and the community; adultery and the position of women; the American past and the failure of utopia.
historical_significance: Hawthorne is the first major American novelist and the central writer of the American romance: The Scarlet Letter is the founding novel of American literature, his tales created the American short story of moral mystery, and his influence runs through Melville, James, Faulkner and O'Connor.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Fanshawe (1828); Twice-Told Tales (1837); Grandfather's Chair (1841); Mosses from an Old Manse (1846); The Snow-Image and Other Twice-Told Tales (1851); The Scarlet Letter (1850); The House of the Seven Gables (1851); A Wonder-Book for Girls and Boys (1852); The Blithedale Romance (1852); Tanglewood Tales (1853); Life of Franklin Pierce (1852); The Marble Faun (1860); Our Old Home (1863); Septimius Felton (unfinished, 1872, posthumous); The Dolliver Romance (unfinished, 1876, posthumous).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the epic romance, the sea narrative and the short story
literary_identity: Novelist, poet and short-story writer; the author of Moby-Dick and the greatest American writer of the sea.
biography: Born in New York City on 1 August 1819; his father's bankruptcy and death in 1832 ended his schooling, and he went to sea in 1839 on a merchant ship and in 1841 on the whaler Acushnet, from which he deserted in the Marquesas in 1842. Typee (1846) and Omoo (1847) made him famous as a writer of the South Seas; Moby-Dick (1851) failed, Pierre (1852) scandalised, and after The Confidence-Man (1857) he wrote almost nothing but poetry and the posthumous Billy Budd. He worked as a customs inspector in New York from 1866 and died there on 28 September 1891.
literary_profile: Melville wrote the American epic against the American romance: Moby-Dick is at once a whaling narrative, an encyclopaedia of cetology, a tragedy of obsession and a metaphysical argument, and its prose is the most various in nineteenth-century American writing — Shakespearean soliloquy, comic catalogue, sermon, stage direction and lyric. His later work turns to the short story and to poetry, and 'Bartleby' and Billy Budd are among the most haunting things in the language.
stylistic_characteristics: Encyclopaedic digression and catalogue; Shakespearean soliloquy and aside; multiple narrative genres inside one book; symbol and emblem pushed to the point of allegory; alliteration and blank-verse cadence in prose; irony and black comedy.
intellectual_concerns: The whale and the sea as metaphysical absolutes; obsession and the will; race, slavery and the crew of the Pequod; the failure of American democracy; the artist and a hostile market; innocence and the law ('Bartleby', Billy Budd); the Pacific and the colonial encounter.
historical_significance: Melville is the greatest of American writers and Moby-Dick the central American book: unread in his lifetime, rediscovered in the 1920s, it is now the foundational text of American studies and of the criticism of empire, race and the sublime. Billy Budd and 'Bartleby' are permanent parts of the world's short fiction.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Typee: A Peep at Polynesian Life (1846); Omoo: A Narrative of Adventures in the South Seas (1847); Mardi: and a Voyage Thither (1849); Redburn: His First Voyage (1849); White-Jacket; or, The World in a Man-of-War (1850); Moby-Dick; or, The Whale (1851); Pierre; or, The Ambiguities (1852); Israel Potter: His Fifty Years of Exile (1855); The Piazza Tales (1856: 'Bartleby', 'Benito Cereno', 'The Encantadas'); The Confidence-Man: His Masquerade (1857); Battle-Pieces and Aspects of the War (1866); Clarel: A Poem and Pilgrimage in the Holy Land (1876); John Marr and Other Sailors (1888); Timoleon (1891); Billy Budd, Sailor (unfinished; 1924, posthumous).

birthplace: West Hills, Long Island, New York, United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the free-verse epic and the democratic lyric
literary_identity: Poet, journalist and essayist; the inventor of American free verse and the poet of American democracy.
biography: Born at West Hills, Long Island, on 31 May 1819; he left school at eleven, worked as a printer's devil, a schoolmaster and a journalist, and edited the Brooklyn Eagle (1846-48) and the New Orleans Crescent (1848). He set the type for the first edition of Leaves of Grass himself in 1855; Emerson's letter of praise made him known. During the Civil War he nursed wounded soldiers in Washington hospitals, and after a stroke in 1873 he lived in Camden, New Jersey. He died there on 26 March 1892.
literary_profile: Whitman invented a poetry for the American continent: long unrhymed lines generated by the breath and by the catalogue, an inclusive vocabulary that admits the technical, the vulgar and the democratic, and a first-person speaker who is at once an individual body and a national 'I'. Leaves of Grass grew through nine editions in his lifetime and is the founding book of modern American poetry.
stylistic_characteristics: Free verse built on syntactical parallelism and anaphora; catalogue and inventory; the long breath-line; first-person address to the reader; colloquial and technical diction; the poem as a growing organism revised across a lifetime.
intellectual_concerns: Democracy, equality and 'the common man'; the body, sex and physical life; death and immortality; the Civil War and Lincoln; comradeship and the love of men; America as the future of the race; the poet as national voice.
historical_significance: Whitman is the founder of modern American poetry and one of the most influential poets in the world: Leaves of Grass changed the possibilities of verse in English, his Civil War poems are the finest written by an American, and his influence runs through Hopkins, Crane, Hart Crane, Neruda, Ginsberg and the Beat generation.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Franklin Evans; or, The Inebriate (novel, 1842); Leaves of Grass (1855; nine editions to 1891-92); Drum-Taps (1865); Sequel to Drum-Taps (1865-66, including 'When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd'); Democratic Vistas (1871); Passage to India (1871); As a Strong Bird on Pinions Free (1872); Memoranda During the War (1875-76); Two Rivulets (1876); Specimen Days (1882); November Boughs (1888); Good-Bye My Fancy (1891); The Complete Prose Works (1892); The Collected Writings (1961-, posthumous).
